name: Akan traditional religion (Nyame/abosom/asamanfo)

dating.dating_summary: The tripartite Nyame/abosom/asamanfo structure as commonly taught is substantially a 20th-century scholarly codification (Danquah 1944, Rattray 1923/1927, Opoku 1978) layered onto older, undated oral-ritual practice; earliest identified written attestation is Willem Bosman's 1704/1705 Dutch trading account; no archaeological or oral-origin date can be assigned with precision.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: UNKNOWN specifically for this cosmological system; Akan shrine-site archaeology exists but no dated find-specific attestation of Nyame/abosom worship was verified in this research pass.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Willem Bosman, A New and Accurate Description of the Coast of Guinea (Dutch 1704, English 1705) — an outside/colonial-trade observer's account, later quoted by Rattray.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Thomas Bowdich (1819), Joseph Dupuis (1824), then R.S. Rattray's early-20th-century fieldwork (Ashanti 1923; Religion and Art in Ashanti 1927), then Danquah (1944).

estimated_composition.method: The scholarly codification into the Nyame/abosom/asamanfo tripartite structure is substantially a 20th-century interpretive product (Danquah explicitly used Christian/Greek monotheistic categories as his comparative frame, per Fighting Words, Peter Lang 2017) layered onto older practice — this is a reasonable reading of the historiography, not a scholar's own verbatim claim.

tradition_internal_claim.note: Presented as coextensive with Akan peoplehood itself; no origin point is claimed.

estimated_oral_origin.method: Linguistic (shared vocabulary for Nyame-type high gods across Kwa-language-family Akan-related groups) would suggest deep pre-colonial antiquity, but no scholar in this research offered a specific glottochronological or archaeological date.

notes: J.B. Danquah, The Akan Doctrine of God (1944; 2nd ed. 1968) — Danquah himself an anticolonial political-intellectual figure (co-founder UGCC, died in Nkrumah-era detention 1965), not a neutral ethnographer; his monotheism-framing of Nyame/Onyankopon/Odomankoma/Borebore is now itself subject to critique. R.S. Rattray, Religion and Art in Ashanti (Oxford, 1927). Anthony Ephirim-Donkor, African Religion Defined: A Systematic Study of Ancestor Worship Among the Akan.
